Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Workplace: Workplace, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma

Vignette:
The call came at 3 a.m. while Eli was asleep. His younger brother, David, had collapsed in his apartment, and by the time the paramedics arrived, it was too late. There had been no long illness, no gradual decline—just the sudden, violent collapse of a man in his prime, followed by the frantic, overlapping sounds of a body being rushed away. Eli had never been one to panic, but that night changed the architecture of his world. In the weeks that followed, the sound of distant sirens would lock him in place. When an ambulance passed down his street, he would press his palms flat against the windowsill, breath shallow, convinced the same fate could descend on him or his wife, Clara, without warning. At his job painting residential exteriors, the trigger was less a sound and more the atmosphere of unexpected chaos. During a job on a split-level in Oakridge, a contractor’s phone rang with the news of a sudden workplace injury. Eli dropped his roller, his shoulders hiking to his ears, the familiar tightening in his chest flooding his limbs with a rigid readiness to flee. Conversations about loss became equally dangerous. At a family barbecue, when his cousin began describing the sudden stroke that had taken his mother, Eli found himself gripping his soda can until his knuckles whitened. He could not stay for the rest of the stories; the emotional weight felt like a physical wall, and he slipped away before anyone noticed him gone. Days bled into nights where safety felt like a concept reserved for daylight hours. Eli would lie in bed, eyes fixed on the ceiling, every floorboard creaking in the house reading as a potential breach. His body refused to uncoil; his shoulders ached from months of carrying a coiled spring beneath his ribs. Even in his own study, with the doors locked and the lights dim, he sat with his back to the wall, scanning the room for exits. His mind refused to offer him a single, coherent narrative of David’s death. Some moments arrived as stark, unblinking photographs: the yellow police tape fluttering in the wind, the paramedic’s gloves pressing against David’s neck, the stark white of the hospital corridor. Other times, the event struck without a single picture, just a crushing wave of dread that filled his mouth and throat, leaving him gasping on the living room floor. When he forced himself to speak of it, the words always dissolved into a suffocating grief that left him shaking for hours. Eli found that he stopped recognizing the man in the mirror. The painter who used to measure his days in color palettes and client deadlines now moved through a life that felt fundamentally erased. He withdrew from the crew, declining the usual post-job beers, certain that no one could possibly understand what it meant to wake up and simply feel less. He stopped taking on family gatherings, telling Clara he needed space, though the isolation sat on him like a second skin. He began arriving early to each job site, walking the perimeter twice, testing every extension cord and ladder rung, convinced that his own hands no longer belonged to him. His work slowed; he double-checked paint cans and drop cloths long after the others had packed up, feeling that his life had been shattered beyond repair. It was the accumulated weight of these shifts that finally pushed him through the clinic’s doors. For three months, Eli had been waking at 2 a.m., staring at the wall, feeling the same hollow devastation that had followed him from the hospital to his job sites to his own bed. He was exhausted from guarding every corner of his life, but what frightened him most was the quiet certainty that he would never feel like himself again. He had come to believe that his life had been destroyed by the trauma, yet he walked into that intake room hoping, against every warning his body gave him, that someone might help him find a way back to the floor.
